title: How to Handle Returns and Size Exchanges on Apliiq Apparel
excerpt: A practical returns workflow for cut-and-sew apparel: why generic size charts fail, what to ask for on a claim, and how to cut exchange requests without hurting trust.
body: Returns on print-on-demand apparel are rarely about print quality. They are about fit. A customer orders their usual size, the blank runs small, and the return request lands with a complaint that reads like a product defect. Cut-and-sew and private label garments make this sharper, because you choose the blank, the cut, and the labeling, which means you also own the size expectation the shopper walks in with. Fix the size chart first, because it is the cheapest lever you have. A generic small-medium-large table fails every customer who measures. Publish flat measurements for chest, body length, and sleeve, taken the way a customer takes them, plus the height and weight of the fit model in your product photos. Add one line telling shoppers what to do when they fall between sizes. That single paragraph removes a meaningful share of exchange requests, and it costs an afternoon spent measuring one sample in each size.

Then decide your returns posture before the first order, not after the first dispute. Made-to-order apparel usually cannot go back into inventory, so an unlimited free return policy turns every sizing mistake into a full write-off. An exchange-first policy works better: the customer keeps or returns the first garment per your stated window, and you ship a replacement size once. Write the window, the condition requirements, and who pays return shipping in plain language on the product page and in the post-purchase email. Check /tool/apliiq on DTCwise when comparing how production partners handle remakes and labeling.

Make the claim form do the work. Ask for three specific things: the measurement the customer expected, the measurement they got, and a photo of the garment laid flat. That is enough to tell a true sizing miss from a production defect, and it tells you which blanks are generating the claims. If one blank drives most of the exchanges, the problem is the blank and not the customer, and the fix is a different blank or a corrected chart rather than another apology.

Route defects separately from fit. A seam failure, a print placement error, or a labeling mistake is a production claim and should go to your production partner with the order number and photos attached, on a schedule you actually follow. Fit complaints are merchandising data. Mixing the two is how teams end up negotiating with their supplier over a size chart they should simply fix. Track both in one sheet with columns for SKU, blank, reason, and resolution cost, and review it once a month.

Close the loop on the catalog. After two or three months of claims you will know which sizes and which blanks cause friction. Retire the offenders, add fit notes to the survivors, and update the photos so the fit model matches the measurements you publish. Returns will not go to zero, and they should not, because a store with no returns is usually a store with a policy customers do not trust. The goal is a returns rate you can predict and price into margin.
